claim: Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area use glutamate as a cotransmitter.
source: Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area use glutamate as a cotransmitter.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about dopamine neurons.

claim: In mice with a dopamine transporter (Slc6a3)-driven conditional heterozygous (cHET) reduction of Gls1 in their dopamine neurons, dopamine neuron survival and transmission were unaffected.
source: In mice with a dopamine transporter (Slc6a3)-driven conditional heterozygous (cHET) reduction of Gls1 in their dopamine neurons, dopamine neuron survival and transmission were unaffected, while glutamate cotransmission at phasic firing frequencies was reduced, enabling a selective focus on the cotransmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing stereological counts and dopamine release measurements.

claim: Glutamate cotransmission at phasic firing frequencies was reduced in DAT GLS1 cHET mice.
source: In mice with a dopamine transporter (Slc6a3)-driven conditional heterozygous (cHET) reduction of Gls1 in their dopamine neurons, dopamine neuron survival and transmission were unaffected, while glutamate cotransmission at phasic firing frequencies was reduced, enabling a selective focus on the cotransmission.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing reduced EPSCs during burst stimulation.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET mice showed normal emotional and motor behaviors.
source: The mice showed normal emotional and motor behaviors, and an unaffected response to acute amphetamine.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from rotarod, elevated plus maze, and open field tests.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET mice showed an unaffected response to acute amphetamine.
source: The mice showed normal emotional and motor behaviors, and an unaffected response to acute amphetamine.
evidence: This is supported by locomotor activity measurements following acute amphetamine administration.

claim: Amphetamine sensitization was reduced in DAT GLS1 cHET mice.
source: Strikingly, amphetamine sensitization was reduced and latent inhibition potentiated.
evidence: This is supported by repeated amphetamine administration experiments showing reduced locomotor sensitization.

claim: Latent inhibition was potentiated in DAT GLS1 cHET mice.
source: Strikingly, amphetamine sensitization was reduced and latent inhibition potentiated.
evidence: This is supported by fear conditioning experiments showing reduced freezing in pre-exposed groups.

claim: The behavioral effects of reduced amphetamine sensitization and potentiated latent inhibition were also seen in global GLS1 HETs with a schizophrenia resilience phenotype.
source: These behavioral effects, also seen in global GLS1 HETs with a schizophrenia resilience phenotype, were not seen in mice with an Emx1-driven forebrain reduction affecting most brain glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from stopGLS1 HET and ΔGLS1 HET mice.

claim: The behavioral effects of reduced amphetamine sensitization and potentiated latent inhibition were not seen in mice with an Emx1-driven forebrain reduction affecting most brain glutamatergic neurons.
source: These behavioral effects, also seen in global GLS1 HETs with a schizophrenia resilience phenotype, were not seen in mice with an Emx1-driven forebrain reduction affecting most brain glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from EMX1 GLS1 cHET mice showing normal sensitization and no LI potentiation.

claim: A reduction in dopamine neuron glutamate cotransmission appears to mediate significant components of the GLS1 HET schizophrenia resilience phenotype.
source: Thus, a reduction in dopamine neuron glutamate cotransmission appears to mediate significant components of the GLS1 HET schizophrenia resilience phenotype, and glutamate cotransmission appears to be important in attribution of motivational salience.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of behavioral phenotypes across different conditional knockout models.

claim: Glutamate cotransmission appears to be important in attribution of motivational salience.
source: Thus, a reduction in dopamine neuron glutamate cotransmission appears to mediate significant components of the GLS1 HET schizophrenia resilience phenotype, and glutamate cotransmission appears to be important in attribution of motivational salience.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral effects on amphetamine sensitization and latent inhibition, which are related to salience processing.

claim: Dopamine neurons regulate several aspects of motivated behaviors (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Salamone and Correa, 2012; Schultz, 2013).
source: Dopamine (DA) neurons regulate several aspects of motivated behaviors (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Salamone and Correa, 2012; Schultz, 2013), and are involved in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders ranging from drug dependence to schizophrenia (Robinson and Berridge, 2008; Winton-Brown et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dopamine neurons are involved in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders ranging from drug dependence to schizophrenia (Robinson and Berridge, 2008; Winton-Brown et al., 2014).
source: Dopamine (DA) neurons regulate several aspects of motivated behaviors (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Salamone and Correa, 2012; Schultz, 2013), and are involved in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders ranging from drug dependence to schizophrenia (Robinson and Berridge, 2008; Winton-Brown et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most CNS neurons release multiple neurotransmitters (Trudeau et al., 2014).
source: Like most CNS neurons, DA neurons release multiple neurotransmitters (Trudeau et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Dopamine neurons release DA with both slower modulatory actions (Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012), as well as faster signaling actions (Ford et al., 2009; Chuhma et al., 2014).
source: They release DA with both slower modulatory actions (Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012), as well as faster signaling actions (Ford et al., 2009; Chuhma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dopamine neurons variously release glutamate (Hnasko and Edwards, 2012) and GABA (Tritsch et al., 2016) as cotransmitters.
source: They variously release glutamate (GLU) (Hnasko and Edwards, 2012) and GABA (Tritsch et al., 2016) as cotransmitters, conferring both greater dynamic signaling range and heterogeneity in their synaptic actions, as well as differential susceptibility to endogenous and exogenous modulation (Chuhma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The abrogation of GLU cotransmission via a DA transporter (DAT)-driven conditional knockout (cKO) of vesicular GLU transporter 2 (VGLUT2, encoded by Slc17a6) (Hnasko et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2010) impairs survival and axonal arborization of DA neurons in vitro.
source: The abrogation of GLU cotransmission via a DA transporter (DAT)-driven conditional knockout (cKO) of vesicular GLU transporter 2 (VGLUT2, encoded by Slc17a6) (Hnasko et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2010) impairs survival and axonal arborization of DA neurons in vitro, and compromises the development of the mesostriatal DA system in vivo leading to a 20% decrease in the number of DA neurons (Fortin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The abrogation of GLU cotransmission via DAT VGLUT2 cKO compromises the development of the mesostriatal DA system in vivo leading to a 20% decrease in the number of DA neurons (Fortin et al., 2012).
source: The abrogation of GLU cotransmission via a DA transporter (DAT)-driven conditional knockout (cKO) of vesicular GLU transporter 2 (VGLUT2, encoded by Slc17a6) (Hnasko et al., 2010; Stuber et al., 2010) impairs survival and axonal arborization of DA neurons in vitro, and compromises the development of the mesostriatal DA system in vivo leading to a 20% decrease in the number of DA neurons (Fortin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DAT VGLUT2 cKO show about a 25% reduction in electrically-evoked DA release and about a 35% reduction in DA content in the nucleus accumbens (Hnasko et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012).
source: Functionally, DAT VGLUT2 cKO show about a 25% reduction in electrically-evoked DA release and about a 35% reduction in DA content in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) (Hnasko et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DAT VGLUT2 cKO show modest deficits in emotional and motor behaviors (Birgner et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012).
source: Behaviorally, DAT VGLUT2 cKO show modest deficits in emotional and motor behaviors (Birgner et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012), normal reinforcement learning drive by DA neuron activation but decreased response vigor (Wang et al., 2017), a blunted response to psychostimulants (Birgner et al., 2010; Hnasko et al., 2010), and a paradoxical increase in sucrose and cocaine seeking (Alsiö et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DAT VGLUT2 cKO show normal reinforcement learning drive by DA neuron activation but decreased response vigor (Wang et al., 2017).
source: Behaviorally, DAT VGLUT2 cKO show modest deficits in emotional and motor behaviors (Birgner et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012), normal reinforcement learning drive by DA neuron activation but decreased response vigor (Wang et al., 2017), a blunted response to psychostimulants (Birgner et al., 2010; Hnasko et al., 2010), and a paradoxical increase in sucrose and cocaine seeking (Alsiö et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DAT VGLUT2 cKO show a blunted response to psychostimulants (Birgner et al., 2010; Hnasko et al., 2010).
source: Behaviorally, DAT VGLUT2 cKO show modest deficits in emotional and motor behaviors (Birgner et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012), normal reinforcement learning drive by DA neuron activation but decreased response vigor (Wang et al., 2017), a blunted response to psychostimulants (Birgner et al., 2010; Hnasko et al., 2010), and a paradoxical increase in sucrose and cocaine seeking (Alsiö et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DAT VGLUT2 cKO show a paradoxical increase in sucrose and cocaine seeking (Alsiö et al., 2011).
source: Behaviorally, DAT VGLUT2 cKO show modest deficits in emotional and motor behaviors (Birgner et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012), normal reinforcement learning drive by DA neuron activation but decreased response vigor (Wang et al., 2017), a blunted response to psychostimulants (Birgner et al., 2010; Hnasko et al., 2010), and a paradoxical increase in sucrose and cocaine seeking (Alsiö et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Phasic activity of DA neurons projecting to the NAc encodes the incentive salience of reward-predicting cues and invigorates cue-induced motivated behaviors (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Flagel et al., 2011).
source: Phasic activity of DA neurons projecting to the NAc encodes the incentive salience of reward-predicting cues and invigorates cue-induced motivated behaviors (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Flagel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DA neurons make the strongest GLU connections in the NAc shell to cholinergic interneurons (Chuhma et al., 2014; Mingote et al., 2015).
source: At the synaptic level in the striatum, DA neurons make the strongest GLU connections in the NAc shell to cholinergic interneurons (ChIs) (Chuhma et al., 2014; Mingote et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When DA neurons are driven at burst firing frequencies, their GLU postsynaptic actions drive synchronized burst-pause sequences in ChIs (Chuhma et al., 2014).
source: When DA neurons are driven at burst firing frequencies — mimicking their in vivo phasic firing — their GLU postsynaptic actions drive synchronized burst-pause sequences in ChIs (Chuhma et al., 2014) that are likely to be important in salience encoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulated DA neuron firing is thought to disrupt salience processing leading to the development of psychotic symptoms (Kapur, 2003; Winton-Brown et al., 2014).
source: Dysregulated DA neuron firing is thought to disrupt salience processing leading to the development of psychotic symptoms (Kapur, 2003; Winton-Brown et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The hyperdopaminergic state associated with positive symptoms of schizophrenia is modeled in rodents by amphetamine sensitization (Peleg-Raibstein et al., 2008).
source: The hyperdopaminergic state associated with positive symptoms of schizophrenia is modeled in rodents by amphetamine sensitization (Peleg-Raibstein et al., 2008), which enhances the motivational salience of drug-associated stimuli (Robinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Amphetamine sensitization enhances the motivational salience of drug-associated stimuli (Robinson et al., 2016).
source: The hyperdopaminergic state associated with positive symptoms of schizophrenia is modeled in rodents by amphetamine sensitization (Peleg-Raibstein et al., 2008), which enhances the motivational salience of drug-associated stimuli (Robinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Amphetamine sensitization and gestational MAM treatment selectively enhance activity of VTA neurons projecting to NAc shell (Lodge and Grace, 2012).
source: Interestingly, amphetamine sensitization as well as gestational MAM treatment, a validated rodent model of schizophrenia, selectively enhance activity of VTA neurons projecting to NAc shell (Lodge and Grace, 2012), a key brain region associated with motivational salience (Ikemoto, 2007), where DA neurons make the strongest GLU connections (Mingote et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The NAc shell is a key brain region associated with motivational salience (Ikemoto, 2007).
source: Interestingly, amphetamine sensitization as well as gestational MAM treatment, a validated rodent model of schizophrenia, selectively enhance activity of VTA neurons projecting to NAc shell (Lodge and Grace, 2012), a key brain region associated with motivational salience (Ikemoto, 2007), where DA neurons make the strongest GLU connections (Mingote et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation in salience processing is thought to underlie the disruption of latent inhibition seen in schizophrenia (Weiner, 2003).
source: Dysregulation in salience processing is also thought to underlie the disruption of latent inhibition (LI) seen in schizophrenia (Weiner, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of LI is replicated in rodents by amphetamine-induced increases in DA neuron activity (Young et al., 2005).
source: Disruption of LI is replicated in rodents by amphetamine-induced increases in DA neuron activity (Young et al., 2005), in particular increases in DA neuron phasic firing (Covey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of LI is replicated in rodents by increases in DA neuron phasic firing (Covey et al., 2016).
source: Disruption of LI is replicated in rodents by amphetamine-induced increases in DA neuron activity (Young et al., 2005), in particular increases in DA neuron phasic firing (Covey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most presynaptic GLU arises from the action of PAG (Marx et al., 2015).
source: Most presynaptic GLU arises from the action of PAG; once released, GLU is taken up by neighboring astrocytes, metabolized to glutamine, and transferred back to presynaptic terminals where it is converted to GLU by PAG (Marx et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The GLU–glutamine cycle is particularly important in sustaining GLU release with higher frequency firing (Billups et al., 2013; Tani et al., 2014).
source: This GLU–glutamine cycle is particularly important in sustaining GLU release with higher frequency firing (Billups et al., 2013; Tani et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deletion (Masson et al., 2006) or heterozygous reduction of Gls1 (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b) decreases GLU neurotransmission at higher firing frequencies selectively.
source: Indeed, deletion (Masson et al., 2006) or heterozygous reduction of Gls1 (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b) decreases GLU neurotransmission at higher firing frequencies selectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The global heterozygous Gls1 reduction impacts several DA dependent behaviors that underpin a schizophrenia resilience phenotype (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b).
source: The global heterozygous Gls1 reduction impacts several DA dependent behaviors that underpin a schizophrenia resilience phenotype (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b), characterized by an attenuated response to psychostimulant challenge, potentiated latent inhibition, procognitive effects (Hazan and Gaisler-Salomon, 2014), together with CA1 hippocampal hypoactivity inverse to the CA1 hyperactivity seen in patients with schizophrenia (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009a; Schobel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The schizophrenia resilience phenotype of global GLS1 HETs is characterized by an attenuated response to psychostimulant challenge, potentiated latent inhibition, procognitive effects (Hazan and Gaisler-Salomon, 2014), together with CA1 hippocampal hypoactivity inverse to the CA1 hyperactivity seen in patients with schizophrenia (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009a; Schobel et al., 2009).
source: The global heterozygous Gls1 reduction impacts several DA dependent behaviors that underpin a schizophrenia resilience phenotype (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b), characterized by an attenuated response to psychostimulant challenge, potentiated latent inhibition, procognitive effects (Hazan and Gaisler-Salomon, 2014), together with CA1 hippocampal hypoactivity inverse to the CA1 hyperactivity seen in patients with schizophrenia (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009a; Schobel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DA neurons immunoreactive for PAG are found in both the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) in rat (Kaneko et al., 1990).
source: DA neurons immunoreactive for PAG are found in both the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) in rat (Kaneko et al., 1990), but this has not been examined in mouse.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Stereological counts in P25 mice showed that TH+/PAG+, TH-/PAG+, and TH+/PAG- cell populations were present in similar proportions in the VTA and SNc.
source: Stereological counts in P25 mice showed that the three cell populations were present in similar proportions in the VTA and SNc (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: DA neurons expressing VGLUT2 are concentrated in the medial VTA (Yamaguchi et al., 2015).
source: In contrast, DA neurons expressing VGLUT2 are concentrated in the medial VTA (Yamaguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TH+/VGLUT2+ neurons preferentially expressed PAG (9 out of 11 TH+/VGLUT2+ cells coexpressed PAG).
source: Importantly, TH+ / VGLUT2+ neurons preferentially expressed PAG (9 out of 11 TH+ / VGLUT2+ cells coexpressed PAG; χ2 =3.6, p=0.035), further supporting the role of PAG in GLU cotransmission (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The number of TH+/PAG+ neurons in both the VTA and SNc increased modestly with age from P25 to P60.
source: The number of PAG+ / TH+ neurons in both the VTA and SNc increased modestly with age (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological data comparing juvenile and adult mice presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The acute locomotor response to amphetamine was not affected in DATIREScre HET mice.
source: DAT and other DA neuron specific gene expression is not affected in the ventral midbrain and striatum of DATIREScre HET mice (Bäckman et al., 2006), which we confirmed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A); the acute locomotor response to amphetamine, a drug that targets DAT function, was also not affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Gls1 expression from the floxGls1 allele is normal (Mingote et al., 2016).
source: We have shown previously that Gls1 expression from the floxGls1 allele is normal (Mingote et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: PCR screens of genomic DNA showed the non-functional truncated (Δ) Gls1 allele in the ventral midbrain of DAT GLS1 cKO mice, but not in forebrain regions.
source: PCR screens of genomic DNA showed the non-functional truncated (Δ) Gls1 allele in the ventral midbrain of DAT GLS1 cKO mice, but not in forebrain regions that do not contain DA neurons, the dorsal striatum (dStr), frontal cortex and hippocampus (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: In DAT GLS1 cKO mice, Gls1 mRNA was absent in VTA cells expressing TH mRNA.
source: In DAT GLS1 cKO mice, Gls1 mRNA was absent in VTA cells expressing TH mRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no impact on the number of DA neurons that expressed VGLUT2 in DAT GLS1 cKO mice (3/38 in DATIREScre/+ vs. 6/30 DAT GLS1 cKO mice).
source: There was no impact on the number of DA neurons that expressed VGLUT2 (3/38 in DATIREScre/+ vs. 6/30 DAT GLS1 cKO mice, χ2 =1.2, p=0.27).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RT-PCR data.

claim: In DAT GLS1 cKO mice, all TH+ cells were PAG-, while neighboring TH- but PAG+ cells were seen.
source: In DAT GLS1 cKO mice, all TH+ cells were PAG—, while neighboring TH— but PAG+ cells were seen, demonstrating the specificity of Gls1 targeting.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of ChR2-EYFP was specific to DA neurons independent of Gls1 genotype.
source: We confirmed that the expression of ChR2-EYFP was specific to DA neurons independent of Gls1 genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and stereological data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: TH+/DAT- striatal interneurons (Xenias et al., 2015) do not express ChR2-EYFP.
source: We also confirmed that TH+ / DAT— striatal interneurons (Xenias et al., 2015) do not express ChR2-EYFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The intrinsic membrane properties of ChIs and SPNs did not differ between genotypes.
source: We confirmed that the intrinsic membrane properties of ChIs and SPNs did not differ between genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C,D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C,D,E.

claim: The amplitude of single-evoked EPSCs was unaffected in cHET mice.
source: The amplitude of single-evoked EPSCs was unaffected in cHET mice (ChIs 66.1 ± 6.7 pA; SPNs 21.2 ± 2.3 pA) (Figure 3B), as were EPSC rise and decay time constants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: Burst-induced EPSCs in ChIs and SPNs showed short-term depression in both genotypes that was significantly greater in cHETs.
source: Burst-induced EPSCs in ChIs and SPNs showed short-term depression in both genotypes that was significantly greater in cHETs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The average amplitude and frequency of spontaneous EPSCs showed no genotypic difference.
source: The average amplitude and frequency of spontaneous EPSCs, measured in both the SPNs and ChIs, showed no genotypic difference (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H,I), indicating that GLU inputs mostly from forebrain regions, as well as signaling through postsynaptic GLU receptors, was unaffected in DAT GLS1 cHETs.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H,I.

claim: DA neuron control of ChI firing in the medial NAc shell was attenuated in cHET mice.
source: At the striatal circuit level, DA neuron control of ChI firing in the medial NAc shell (Chuhma et al., 2014) was attenuated in cHET mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3D and a citation to previous literature.

claim: There were no genotypic differences in baseline firing frequencies of ChIs (CTRL 4.7 ± 1.1 Hz; cHET 3.9 ± 0.6 Hz).
source: There were no genotypic differences in baseline firing frequencies (CTRL 4.7 ± 1.1 Hz; cHET 3.9 ± 0.6 Hz; ANOVA, F(1,33)= 0.60, p=0.444).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The firing ratio during train photostimulation in CTRL mice was 4.3 ± 0.7 compared to 2.1 ± 0.2 in cHET mice, which was significantly reduced.
source: The firing ratio in CTRL mice was 4.3 ± 0.7 compared to 2.1 ± 0.2 in cHET mice, which was significantly reduced (Figure 3D, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: There was no reduction in the number of DA neurons in the VTA or SNc in DAT GLS1 cHETs at P110.
source: We found no reduction in the number of DA neurons in the VTA (unilateral counts: CTRL 7548 ± 418, cHET 7310 ± 450) or SNc (CTRL 6595 ± 373, cHET 6781 ± 518).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: DA neurons in cHET mice showed no differences in their intrinsic electrophysiological properties.
source: DA neurons in cHET mice showed no differences in their intrinsic electrophysiological properties (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Presynaptic DA content and turnover in the NAc and dStr of adult mice did not significantly differ between genotypes.
source: Presynaptic DA content and turnover, in the NAc and dStr of adult mice (P71-P110), did not significantly differ between genotypes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: There were no genotypic differences in DA release with either single or burst photostimulation in the NAc medial shell.
source: There were no genotypic differences in DA release with either stimulation pattern (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: The decay time constant of DA responses did not differ significantly between genotypes with single or burst photostimulation.
source: The decay time constant of DA responses did not differ significantly between genotypes with single (CTRL 409 ± 30 ms; cHET 362 ± 26 ms; ANOVA,F(1,23)=1.42, p=0.245) or burst photostimulation (CTRL 540 ± 28 ms; cHET 482 ± 25 ms; ANOVA, F(1,22)= 2.12, p=0.160).
evidence: This claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data.

claim: Evoked DA release was not affected in the NAc core or dStr in DAT GLS1 cHETs.
source: Evoked DA release was not affected in the NAc core (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B,C) nor in the dStr (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E,F), indicating that DA storage and release dynamics throughout the striatum are normal in DAT GLS1 cHETs.
evidence: This claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET mice showed robust motor learning on the rotarod, which did not differ from CTRL mice.
source: DAT GLS1 cHET mice showed robust motor learning, which did not differ from CTRL mice, on the first training day, when rotarod speed was 20 rpm (Figure 5A), and then accelerated to 30 rpm and 40 rpm on subsequent days.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Novelty-induced exploration in the open field was unaffected in DAT GLS1 cHET mice.
source: Novelty-induced exploration in the open field was unaffected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET and CTRL mice spent the same time in the center of the open field.
source: DAT GLS1 cHET and CTRL mice spent the same time in the center of the open field (CTRL = 256± 43 s; DAT GLS1 cHET = 301 ± 23 s; one-way ANOVA, no genotype effect, F(1,102) = 0.551, p=0.46).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET and CTRL mice spent the same time in the open arms of the elevated plus maze.
source: We found no difference between genotypes in the time spent in the open arms, nor was there a difference between time spent in the open arms per entry (Figure 5C), or the time spent in the proximal and distal portions of the longer arms (proximal time, CTRL = 47.4 ± 4.4 s, cHET = 40.9 ± 4.9 s, one-way ANOVA, no genotype effect, F(1,24) = 0.887, p=0.36; distal time, CTRL = 43.7 ± 8.5 s, cHET = 51.27 ± 7.90 s, F(1.24) = 0.41, p=0.53).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET mice showed normal tone- and context-dependent fear conditioning.
source: However, DAT GLS1 cHET mice showed normal tone- and context-dependent fear conditioning (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET mice responded to low (2.5 mg/Kg) and high (5 mg/Kg) doses of amphetamine indistinguishably from CTRL mice.
source: DAT GLS1 cHET mice responded to low (2.5 mg/Kg) and high (5 mg/Kg) doses of amphetamine indistinguishably from CTRL mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: With daily amphetamine injections over 5 days, CTRL mice showed an increase in drug-induced hyperlocomotion, characteristic of a sensitized response, while cHET mice showed no increase in hyperlocomotion.
source: With daily amphetamine injections (2.5 mg/kg) over 5 days, CTRL mice showed an increase in drug-induced hyperlocomotion, characteristic of a sensitized response (Figure 6B), while cHET mice showed no increase in hyperlocomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: During the amphetamine challenge, amphetamine-treated CTRL mice showed a significant sensitized response, while amphetamine-treated cHET mice showed a significant but smaller sensitized response.
source: During the amphetamine challenge, amphetamine-treated CTRL mice showed a significant sensitized response, while amphetamine-treated cHET mice showed a significant but smaller sensitized response (Figure 6B, gray area).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: CTRL mice showed increased freezing during CS presentation with no difference between the NPE and PE groups, revealing no LI.
source: During CS presentation, CTRL mice showed increased freezing with no difference between the NPE and PE groups (Figure 6E, left graph), revealing the learned tone-fear association and no LI.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: The cHET PE group showed less freezing in comparison to the NPE group during CS presentation, revealing potentiated LI.
source: In contrast, the cHET PE group showed less freezing in comparison to the NPE group, revealing potentiated LI (Figure 6E, right graph).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: The cHET NPE group did not differ from the CTRL NPE group, showing that aversive associative learning per se was not affected in cHETs.
source: Importantly, when analyzing the total freezing during the CS presentation and comparing responses between genotypes directly, the cHET NPE group did not differ from the CTRL NPE group, showing that aversive associative learning per se was not affected in cHETs (Figure 6F), replicating previous findings (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6F and comparison to Figure 5D.

claim: EMX1 GLS1 cHETs did not differ from CTRL mice in their novelty-induced locomotion in the open field.
source: EMX1 GLS1 cHETs (P85-107) did not differ from CTRL mice in their novelty-induced locomotion in the open field (Figure 6H) and amphetamine sensitization (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6H.

claim: EMX1 GLS1 cHETs did not differ from CTRL mice in amphetamine sensitization.
source: EMX1 GLS1 cHETs (P85-107) did not differ from CTRL mice in their novelty-induced locomotion in the open field (Figure 6H) and amphetamine sensitization (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6I.

claim: EMX1 GLS1 cHETs did not show potentiation of LI.
source: EMX1 GLS1 cHETs (P80-96) did not show potentiation of LI (ES for nonsignificant PE X genotype interaction = 0.016) (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6J.

claim: In both CTRL and EMX1 GLS1 cHETs, clozapine treatment on Day 1 potentiated LI in the PE groups.
source: In both CTRL and EMX1 GLS1 cHETs, clozapine treatment on Day 1, potentiated LI in the PE groups (Figure 6—figure supplement 5B), but had no effect in the NPE groups showing that it did not affect learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Similar clozapine effects were seen in ΔGLS1 HET and DAT GLS1 cHET mice.
source: Similar clozapine effects were seen in ΔGLS1 HET and DAT GLS1 cHET mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 5C.

claim: About half of DA neurons express PAG in both the VTA and SNc.
source: A stereological analysis of PAG expression in DA neurons revealed that about half of DA neurons express PAG in both the VTA and SNc, in contrast to VGLUT2 expression, which is mostly restricted to DA neurons in the VTA (Yamaguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological data presented in Figure 1C and a citation to previous literature.

claim: A minor reduction of PAG expression in SNc DA neurons had no impact on their survival or intrinsic physiology, nor did it affect DA transmission in the dStr or motor behaviors controlled by the dStr.
source: The function of PAG in SNc DA neurons incapable of GLU cotransmission is still uncertain, although we show that a minor reduction of PAG expression in those neurons had no impact on their survival or intrinsic physiology, nor did it affect DA transmission in the dStr or motor behaviors controlled by the dStr.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing normal DA neuron counts, DA release in dStr, and motor behaviors.

claim: A reduction of PAG in VTA DA neurons capable of GLU cotransmission was sufficient to attenuate phasic GLU cotransmission in the NAc shell and impact behaviors controlled by the NAc.
source: In contrast, DA neurons capable of GLU cotransmission (TH+ / VGLUT2+ cells) preferentially express PAG, and a reduction of PAG in those VTA DA neurons was sufficient to attenuate phasic GLU cotransmission in the NAc shell and impact behaviors controlled by the NAc, revealing the important role of PAG in DA neuron GLU cotransmission.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology and behavioral data showing reduced EPSCs and altered behaviors.

claim: The reduction in PAG activity of about 20% seen in stopGLS1 HET brain slices (El Hage et al., 2012) is associated with about a 15% reduction in GLU content (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b).
source: The reduction in PAG activity of about 20% seen in stopGLS1 HET brain slices (El Hage et al., 2012) is associated with about a 15% reduction in GLU content (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b) that presumably reflects a presynaptic diminution, since the highest concentrations of GLU are intracellular (Danbolt, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Decreases in presynaptic GLU lead to decreases in vesicular GLU content and synaptic efficacy (Ishikawa et al., 2002).
source: Decreases in presynaptic GLU lead to decreases in vesicular GLU content and synaptic efficacy (Ishikawa et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In DAT GLS1 cHETs, the first EPSC elicited by burst photostimulation was unaffected, as was observed in cultured GLS1 KO neurons (Masson et al., 2006).
source: In DAT GLS1 cHETs, the first EPSC elicited by burst photostimulation was unaffected, as was observed in cultured GLS1 KO neurons (Masson et al., 2006), indicating that the readily releasable vesicle pool is replete.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data and a citation to previous literature.

claim: PAG expression in VTA DA neurons is weak to moderate relative to other brain regions (Kaneko, 2000).
source: PAG expression in VTA DA neurons is weak to moderate relative to other brain regions (Kaneko, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DA neurons have low VGLUT2 mRNA copy numbers (Trudeau et al., 2014).
source: Single cell RT-PCR studies show that DA neurons also have low VGLUT2 mRNA copy numbers (Trudeau et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Vesicular loading depends both on cytosolic GLU concentration and vesicular transporter number (Wilson et al., 2005).
source: Lower VGLUT2 expression would place further demands on the GLU-glutamine cycle to sustain synaptic transmission during periods of high activity, given that vesicular loading depends both on cytosolic GLU concentration and vesicular transporter number (Wilson et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The global reduction in PAG activity in global GLS1 HETs affects DA neuron GLU cotransmission preferentially.
source: This indicates that the DA neuron GLU cotransmission in DAT GLS1 cHETS is highly dependent on PAG activity, and suggests that the global reduction in PAG activity in global GLS1 HETs affects DA neuron GLU cotransmission preferentially.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of behavioral phenotypes and the biochemical properties of DA neurons.

claim: In DAT VGLUT2 cKOs, DA neuron function is affected profoundly due to the developmental role of VGLUT2 in DA neurons (Fortin et al., 2012).
source: In DAT VGLUT2 cKOs, DA neuron function is affected profoundly due to the developmental role of VGLUT2 in DA neurons (Fortin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In DAT GLS1 cHETs, DA neuron DA functions appear normal; Gls1 reduction affects neither the survival of DA neurons nor their intrinsic electrophysiological properties.
source: In DAT GLS1 cHETs, DA neuron DA functions appear normal; Gls1 reduction affects neither the survival of DA neurons nor their intrinsic electrophysiological properties.
evidence: This is supported by stereological and electrophysiology data presented in Figure 4.

claim: VGLUT2 plays an important role in vesicular DA uptake (Hnasko et al., 2010).
source: VGLUT2 also plays an important role in vesicular DA uptake (Hnasko et al., 2010), but there was no impact of Gls1 deficiency on DA content or release, even when DA terminals were stimulated repeatedly to increase the demand on DA release.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There was no impact of Gls1 deficiency on DA content or release in DAT GLS1 cHETs.
source: VGLUT2 also plays an important role in vesicular DA uptake (Hnasko et al., 2010), but there was no impact of Gls1 deficiency on DA content or release, even when DA terminals were stimulated repeatedly to increase the demand on DA release.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC and voltammetry data presented in Figure 4.

claim: DA neuron GLU release may arise from segregated release sites (Zhang et al., 2015).
source: Alternately, DA neuron GLU release may arise from segregated release sites (Zhang et al., 2015), so reduced vesicular GLU filling would not affect DA release.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is presented as an alternative explanation.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET mice do not show decreased novelty-induced locomotion, motor deficits on the rotarod, an anxiety phenotype, or blunted responses to psychostimulants seen in DAT VGLUT2 cKOs (Birgner et al., 2010; Hnasko et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012).
source: DAT GLS1 cHET mice do not show several behavioral phenotypes of DAT VGLUT2 cKOs, such as decreased novelty-induced locomotion, motor deficits on the rotarod, an anxiety phenotype, or blunted responses to psychostimulants (Birgner et al., 2010; Hnasko et al., 2010; Fortin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5 and citations to previous literature.

claim: DA signaling increases with psychostimulant sensitization (Vezina, 2004; Bocklisch et al., 2013; Covey et al., 2014).
source: DA signaling increases with psychostimulant sensitization (Vezina, 2004; Bocklisch et al., 2013; Covey et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DA neuron excitatory connections to SPNs in the NAc core are modestly but significantly increased weeks after chronic psychostimulant administration (Ishikawa et al., 2013).
source: DA neuron excitatory connections to SPNs in the NAc core are modestly but significantly increased weeks after chronic psychostimulant administration (Ishikawa et al., 2013); psychostimulant-induced plasticity may be even stronger at DA neuron excitatory connections to ChIs in the NAc shell (Chuhma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Psychostimulant-induced plasticity may be even stronger at DA neuron excitatory connections to ChIs in the NAc shell (Chuhma et al., 2014).
source: DA neuron excitatory connections to SPNs in the NAc core are modestly but significantly increased weeks after chronic psychostimulant administration (Ishikawa et al., 2013); psychostimulant-induced plasticity may be even stronger at DA neuron excitatory connections to ChIs in the NAc shell (Chuhma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is presented as speculation.

claim: Reducing GLU cotransmission may attenuate increases in DA neuron activity associated with sensitization (Bocklisch et al., 2013).
source: At the VTA-NAc circuit level, reducing GLU cotransmission may attenuate increases in DA neuron activity associated with sensitization (Bocklisch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and is presented as speculation.

claim: DA neuron activity mediates both amphetamine sensitization and LI by encoding motivational salience of relevant events (Young et al., 2005; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2016).
source: DA neuron activity mediates both amphetamine sensitization and LI by encoding motivational salience of relevant events (Young et al., 2005; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DA neuron GLU signaling plays a key role in salience attribution.
source: Our results suggest that DA neuron GLU signaling plays a key role in salience attribution.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral effects on amphetamine sensitization and latent inhibition.

claim: In amphetamine sensitization, increases in DA neuron firing are restricted to medial VTA DA neurons (Lodge and Grace, 2012), the majority of which are capable of GLU cotransmission (Yamaguchi et al., 2015).
source: In amphetamine sensitization, increases in DA neuron firing are restricted to medial VTA DA neurons (Lodge and Grace, 2012), the majority of which are capable of GLU cotransmission (Yamaguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: All abused drugs increase DA neuron activity to strengthen the motivational salience of drug exposure or associated events (Covey et al., 2014).
source: Recent evidence suggests that all abused drugs increase DA neuron activity to strengthen the motivational salience of drug exposure or associated events (Covey et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DAT GLS1 cHET mice do not show sensitization to amphetamine with repeated administration, and after a withdrawal period show reduced expression of sensitization.
source: DAT GLS1 cHET mice do not show sensitization to amphetamine with repeated administration, and after a withdrawal period show reduced expression of sensitization.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Mice with a conditional NR1 deletion in their DA neurons showed a dramatic reduction in phasic firing (Zweifel et al., 2009).
source: Similar results were found in mice with a conditional NR1 deletion in their DA neurons that resulted in a dramatic reduction in phasic firing (Zweifel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: While the development of sensitization was unaffected in DAT NR1 cKO mice, the mice showed reduced expression of sensitization weeks after withdrawal (Zweifel et al., 2008).
source: While the development of sensitization was unaffected in DAT NR1 cKO mice, the mice showed reduced expression of sensitization weeks after withdrawal (Zweifel et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Phasic DA neuron GLU signals facilitate sensitization by determining how rapidly and efficiently pathological levels of salience are attributed to drug exposure.
source: Taken together, several lines of evidence suggest that phasic DA neuron GLU signals facilitate sensitization by determining how rapidly and efficiently pathological levels of salience are attributed to drug exposure.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of behavioral phenotypes across different models.

claim: DAT NR1 cKO showed a reduction in conditioned responses to context not seen in DAT GLS1 cHET mice.
source: In contrast, DAT NR1 cKO showed a reduction in conditioned responses to context not seen in the present study, suggesting that the abrogation of both DA and GLU phasic transmission must be affected to impact the development of drug-induced conditioned responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of behavioral phenotypes between DAT NR1 cKO and DAT GLS1 cHET mice.

claim: In LI, the activity of DA neurons in the NAc updates the salience of a preexposed stimulus during the conditioning phase by integrating previous with current behavioral experiences (Young et al., 2005).
source: In LI, it is thought that the activity of DA neurons in the NAc updates the salience of a preexposed stimulus during the conditioning phase by integrating previous with current behavioral experiences (Young et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The potentiation of LI seen in DAT GLS1 cHET mice represents a failure of DA neurons to increase the salience of the inconsequential preexposed stimulus under changed reinforcement contingencies during conditioning.
source: Thus, the potentiation of LI seen in DAT GLS1 cHET mice represents a failure of DA neurons to increase the salience of the inconsequential preexposed stimulus under changed reinforcement contingencies during conditioning.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data on latent inhibition.

claim: The temporal precision of the DA neuron GLU signal makes it particularly suitable for updating salience.
source: The temporal precision of the DA neuron GLU signal makes it particularly suitable for updating salience.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of glutamatergic transmission.

claim: Direct optogenetic excitation of ChIs in the NAc shell does not drive reinforcement learning on its own but instead modulates learning (Lee et al., 2016).
source: Direct optogenetic excitation of ChIs in the NAc shell — as would result from DA neuron GLU actions — does not drive reinforcement learning on its own but instead modulates learning (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: GLU cotransmission is not required for self-administration reinforced by DA neuron activation (Wang et al., 2017).
source: It has been recently shown that GLU cotransmission is not required for self-administration reinforced by DA neuron activation (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DA neuron GLU signals modulate learning by regulating the attribution of motivational salience to relevant events via their direct control of ChI activity.
source: Taken together with our behavioral results, this suggests that DA neuron GLU signals modulate learning by regulating the attribution of motivational salience to relevant events via their direct control of ChI activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data and previous literature on ChI function.

claim: The behaviors affected in DAT GLS1 cHETs align with the schizophrenia resilience phenotype of stopGLS1 HET (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b), as well as ΔGLS1 HET mice.
source: In the context of schizophrenia, the behaviors affected in DAT GLS1 cHETs align with the schizophrenia resilience phenotype of stopGLS1 HET (Gaisler-Salomon et al., 2009b), as well as ΔGLS1 HET mice, both with a global GLS1 heterozygous reduction.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from multiple mouse models.

claim: Several phenotypes of GLS1 HETs, including a blunted locomotor response to novelty, diminished sensitivity to acute amphetamine or reduced contextual fear conditioning, were not seen in DAT GLS1 cHETs and so apparently do not depend on GLU cotransmission.
source: Several other phenotypes of GLS1 HETs, a blunted locomotor response to novelty, diminished sensitivity to acute amphetamine or reduced contextual fear conditioning were not seen in DAT GLS1 cHETs and so apparently do not depend on GLU cotransmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of behavioral phenotypes.

claim: None of the behavioral deficits seen in global GLS1 HETs were recapitulated in EMX1 GLS1 cHETs, demonstrating that PAG in DA neurons is necessary for amphetamine sensitization and potentiation of LI.
source: Furthermore, none of these behavioral deficits were recapitulated in EMX1 GLS1 cHETs, with a forebrain-restricted GLS1 reduction, demonstrating that PAG in DA neurons is necessary for amphetamine sensitization and potentiation of LI, and reinforcing the likelihood that DA neuron GLU cotransmission is particularly sensitive to PAG reduction.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from EMX1 GLS1 cHET mice.

claim: Modeling resilience in mice using transgenic approaches offers a direct path to intervention, as resilience mutations point directly to therapeutic targets (Mihali et al., 2012).
source: Modeling resilience in mice using transgenic approaches offers a direct path to intervention, as resilience mutations point directly to therapeutic targets (Mihali et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VGLUT2 expression has been demonstrated in primate DA neurons (Root et al., 2016).
source: Supported by the recent demonstration of VGLUT2 expression — and thus of GLU cotransmission — in primate DA neurons (Root et al., 2016), the therapeutic potential of PAG inhibition as a pharmacotherapy for schizophrenia (Mingote et al., 2016) may involve tempering DA neuron GLU cotransmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The therapeutic potential of PAG inhibition as a pharmacotherapy for schizophrenia (Mingote et al., 2016) may involve tempering DA neuron GLU cotransmission.
source: Supported by the recent demonstration of VGLUT2 expression — and thus of GLU cotransmission — in primate DA neurons (Root et al., 2016), the therapeutic potential of PAG inhibition as a pharmacotherapy for schizophrenia (Mingote et al., 2016) may involve tempering DA neuron GLU cotransmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data and previous literature on PAG inhibition.

claim: An increase in GLU cotransmission in the NAc may contribute to the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, in particular to aberrant salience leading to psychosis.
source: Finally, our findings put forward the possibility that an increase in GLU cotransmission in the NAc may contribute to the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, in particular to aberrant salience leading to psychosis.
evidence: This is presented as speculation based on the findings.

claim: Increased activity in the midbrain and NAc has been associated with aberrant salience attribution to irrelevant stimuli in patients with psychosis or individuals at high risk (Romaniuk et al., 2010; Roiser et al., 2013).
source: Increased activity in the midbrain and NAc has been associated with aberrant salience attribution to irrelevant stimuli in patients with psychosis or individuals at high risk (Romaniuk et al., 2010; Roiser et al., 2013), while increased NAc activity does not correlate with increased dopamine synthesis capacity (Roiser et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased NAc activity does not correlate with increased dopamine synthesis capacity (Roiser et al., 2013).
source: Increased activity in the midbrain and NAc has been associated with aberrant salience attribution to irrelevant stimuli in patients with psychosis or individuals at high risk (Romaniuk et al., 2010; Roiser et al., 2013), while increased NAc activity does not correlate with increased dopamine synthesis capacity (Roiser et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased activity in the VTA and NAc in schizophrenia may be associated with a greater pathological increase in GLU cotransmission than in DA transmission.
source: This inconsistency would be reconciled if increased activity in the VTA and NAc in SCZ is associated with a greater pathological increase in GLU cotransmission than in DA transmission.
evidence: This is presented as speculation to reconcile findings from the literature.
